messages.subject: מפגש R בישראל 2018-05-28
messages.body_plain:
פורסם במקור כאן:
http://r-israel.com/2018/05/248

קישור להרשמה למפגש <https://goo.gl/forms/gek8mqWk0gZ1g96x1>

אנחנו שמחים מאד להזמין אתכם למפגש R אשר יתקיים ב 28.5 (יום שני) ב 19:30 ב start hub, מתחם WeWork <http://starthub.co.il/> אבן גבירול 30 תל אביב (תודה רבה לעומרי מנדלז שעזר ודחף לכך שהמפגש יתקיים).
המפגש הזה מתקיים בזכות צירוף המקרים המשמח לפיו יהיו לנו שני משתמשי R מתקדמים (דין ויוני, ראו פירוט בהמשך) שמגיעים לבקר בישראל בעוד שבועיים, והסכימו לתת לנו הרצאות על העבודה שהם עושים ובכך מציעים לנו מספיק תוכן איכותי שאמור להחזיק מפגש שלם (עמרי ואנוכי ניתן הרצאות משלנו גם כן).
ההרצאות במפגש יתחילו בשעה 19:30 ויסתיימו בסביבות 22:00 (עם הפסקה של חצי שעה באמצע). במפגש יועברו 4 הרצאות (כל אחת בין 20 ל- 30 דקות, אנו צפויים לגלות מידה מסויימת של גמישות),סילבוסים מורחבים בהמשך הפוסט:
What makes an R talk popular? Scraping useR2017 attendance information to find out! – Dean Attali
Sinew: Simple R Package Documentation – Yoni Sidi
Cloud computing with R – Omri Mendels
Highlights from eRum 2018 – Tal Galili
ההשתתפות היא בחינם, אך דורשת הרשמה מוקדמת: עליכם להירשם בגוגל-טופס שמופיע בקישור הישיר כאן <https://goo.gl/forms/gek8mqWk0gZ1g96x1>. יש הגבלת מקום של כ- 100 איש, אז אנא מהרו להירשם <https://goo.gl/forms/gek8mqWk0gZ1g96x1>. לאחר שירשמו 100 הראשונים, ישלח אליהם (כשבוע לקראת המפגש) מייל שמודיע שהם "בפנים". לאחר מכן ההרשמה תישאר פתוחה ל"רשימת המתנה", ובשבוע שלפני הסדנא נברר כמה אנשים לא יוכלו להגיע – ונזמין את האנשים מרשימת ההמתנה להגיע. בד"כ כשליש (לפחות) מהאנשים מבטלים ברגע האחרון, אז הרבה מהאנשים של רשימת ההמתנה צפויים לקבל הזמנה להגיע (אז תירשמו  <https://goo.gl/forms/gek8mqWk0gZ1g96x1> ).
קהל היעד?

משתמשי R עם ניסיון של יותר משנה בתוכנה (חלק מההרצאות יהיו באנגלית).
נושאי המפגש

להלן נושאי ההרצאות:

What makes an R talk popular? Scraping useR2017 attendance information to find out! – Dean Attali
Last summer, the useR! conference in Belgium invited all its attendees to use a scheduling app to mark the sessions they'd like to attend. Since the majority of people at the conference actually used this service and the schedule of each person was public, some interesting data regarding people's R talk preferences can be extracted. Which talks are most anticipated? Which types of session do people prefer the most? To answer these questions, the full scheduling data can be scraped with R and presented with a Shiny app to make it easy to explore.
About the speaker: https://github.com/daattali

Sinew: Simple R Package Documentation – Yoni Sidi

At the core of creating reproducible research is the daunting process of documentation, and working with R presents no exception. The standardized R package documentation is part of the appeal for new (and experienced) users, where concise, clear instructions are cherished. Packages are great for reusing scripts in a consistent fashion and for developers, package creation helps organizing and maintaining their ideas.
The barrier to entry for package maintenance and documentation, however may be too high for R users embarking on the task of package creation, thereby discouraging them from development. The out-of-the-box roxygen2 skeleton supplied by RStudio gives the bare bones road map of what should be part of function documentation.
The goal of sinew is to automate nearly all of the manual tasks needed to document functions, properly set up the import fields for oxygenation, and make it easier to attain documentation consistency across functions and packages.
Once the initial documentation is set, sinew can be used as part of the natural maintenance workflow to automatically change and append updated parameters, definitions, defaults, add namespacing to functions and dependencies, making your documentation great – again!
About the speaker: https://github.com/yonicd/

Cloud computing with R – Omri Mendels
We'll touch some of the tools available for R developers on Microsoft's cloud, Azure. These tools help R users to set up data science environments (notebooks, r-studio server), handle big data with Spark, run parallel processes, and run machine learning models in R.
About the speaker: Omri Mendels is a Senior Data & Applied Scientist at Microsoft. In his current role he helps different companies solve interesting machine learning and data related problems. The solutions to these problems are then shared with the open source community and on Microsoft's developer blog.

Highlights from eRum 2018 – Tal Galili
The eRum <https://2018.erum.io/> (a.k.a: The European R Users Meeting) is an international conference, similar to useR! <https://www.r-project.org/conferences.html>, that occurs every two years (specifically, in the years in which useR is taking place outside of Europe). Link to the post <https://www.r-statistics.com/2018/04/registration-for-erum-2018-closes-in-two-days/> explaining why I'll go to eRum this year and not useR.
I have no idea what I'll talk about, but I suspect it would be cool.
About the speaker: https://github.com/talgalili/

www.biostatistics.co.il <http://www.biostatistics.co.il/> (Hebrew)  | www.talgalili.com <http://www.talgalili.com/> (Hebrew)

messages.subject_clean: חיסור בין שני עמודות בין dataframe-ים שונים
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lior,
Not sure I understand.
If you have a dataframe df1 with 100 rows and dataframe df2 with 130 rows, what should be the result of subtracting one column from the other?
Basically R supports vector operations so there's no need to write loops. For example, assuming that both data frames have the same number of rows:

z <- df1$x > df2$x

would give you a vector of TRUE and FALSE for each row.

If you subtract to vectors of unequal lengths, you'd get the result only for some rows and a warning message:
> df1 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100))
> df2 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(130))
> z <- (df1$x - df2$x) > 1

Warning message:
In df1$x > df2$x :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

If one data frame has a length that is a multiple of the second (e.g. 100 and 200), R would reuse the smaller vector again:

df1 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100))
df2 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(200))
z <- (df1$x - df2$x) > 1
(no warning message even though df1 and df2 have different lengths).

Hope this helps.
Omri

messages.subject_clean: Count and relative frequencies in dataframe by multiple criteria
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a dataframe (~750,000 rows) containing records of individuals (TransmitterSerial) detected by different receivers (Receiver) over a period of many months.

> head(df)

      Receiver TransmitterSerial       Date     Time Hour Month

1 VR2W-123227           1168793 08/07/2016 14:06:19   14   Jul

2 VR2W-123227           1168793 08/07/2016 14:08:23   14   Jul

3 VR2W-123228           1168793 08/07/2016 14:08:29   14   Jul

4 VR2W-123228           1212923 08/07/2016 14:08:46   14   Jul

5 VR2W-123228           1212923 08/07/2016 14:09:39   14   Jul

6 VR2W-123227           1168793 08/07/2016 14:11:24   14   Jul

I’m trying to summarize the relative frequency of each receiver per individual within hour (HOUR) for each day (DATE).

The requested output (let it be summary_df), would ideally look something like this:

> head(summary_df)

TransmitterSerial  Receiver     Date          Hour     count   relative_freq

1168793            VR2W-123227  08/07/2016    21       45      0.45

1168793            VR2W-885115  08/07/2016    21       6       0.06

1168793            VR2W-320024  08/07/2016    21       49      0.49

1168793            VR2W-123227  08/07/2016    22       147     0.98

1168793            VR2W-320024  08/07/2016    22       3       0.02

I tried using dplyr to group_by(TransmitterSerial, Receiver, Date, Hour) and mutate() to count nrow() per hour and calculate relative_freq by division, but I keep on getting lost in the syntax.   I also tried a for loop to first subset by individual, but no success there either.

Any help would be greatly appreciated, thank you.

messages.body_plain:
The general approach may be something like this -

1. Calculating summary table A, with N = total number of observations per (TransmitterSerial, Date, Hour), using 'group_by' with 'summarize'
2. Calculating summary table B, with n = number of observations per (TransmitterSerial, Receiver, Date, Hour), again using 'group_by' with 'summarize'
3. Using 'left_join(B, A)' to get a table with both the individual count 'n' and total hourly count 'N'
4. Dividing the columns 'n' / 'N', to get a new 'proportion' column

There are surely shorter ways to do it with 'dplyr', but this is the easiest to explain without a specific data example.

> 1. Calculating summary table A, with N = total number of observations per (TransmitterSerial, Date, Hour), using 'group_by' with 'summarize'
> 2. Calculating summary table B, with n = number of observations per (TransmitterSerial, Receiver, Date, Hour), again using 'group_by' with 'summarize'
> 3. Using 'left_join(B, A)' to get a table with both the individual count 'n' and total hourly count 'N'
> 4. Dividing the columns 'n' / 'N', to get a new 'proportion' column
>
> There are surely shorter ways to do it with 'dplyr', but this is the easiest to explain without a specific data example.
>

> On Sun, May 27, 2018 at 12:27 PM, Renanel Pickholtz <renan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> >
> >
> > I’m trying to summarize the relative frequency of each receiver per individual within hour (HOUR) for each day (DATE).
> >
> > The requested output (let it be summary_df), would ideally look something like this:
> >
> >
> > > head(summary_df)
